The geometry of a moving subspace

Intrinsic Quantum Geometric Tensor on the Grassmannian and Spectral Lower Bounds on Dissipation

Jeromie Beasley

Abstract

Reviewer advisory: this paper was created with AI assistance.

We construct a fully coordinate-free formulation of the Quantum Geometric Tensor on the Grassmannian manifold of rank- orthogonal projectors associated with an isolated spectral subspace of a self-adjoint operator on a separable Hilbert space . Starting from Kato's analytic perturbation theory and the Riesz resolvent formula, we define an intrinsic Hermitian form on the tangent bundle of the Grassmannian. Its symmetric real part is the intrinsic Hilbert–Schmidt quantum metric and its skew-symmetric imaginary part is the Berry curvature 2-form. Every tangent deformation is generated by transitions across the spectral gap, and both components admit exact spectral decompositions in terms of inter-band matrix elements weighted by inverse gaps. We prove the sharp metric–curvature inequality in operator form: the determinant inequality of band geometry, extended to any pair of tangent directions on the Grassmannian, with its extremal partner given explicitly. Every bound in the paper is sharp and rigid: equality in the gap bound, the speed limit, the dissipation floor, the curvature bound and the trace condition each forces one recognisable configuration, and the curvature deficit is an exact quadratic form whose kernel is the complex line of the given direction.

For dissipation, the metric is the quantum Fisher information of the moving subspace, and under an explicit bath model the friction on projector rotations is the metric reweighted by the spectrum, which bounds the excess work of finite-time driving from below by the squared intrinsic length over the time allowed; the friction weight is checked against slow-driving simulations of two different baths. Transport tensors, including the quantum metric dipole, the nonlinear Hall response and the orbital moment, arise as pullbacks of one cross-gap pair sum read with different powers of the gap. Across degenerate strata, geodesics of the pullback metric obey a refraction law whose index is the rate at which the subspace rotates: strata where the subspace stops rotating reflect trajectories, while lines where the gap narrows guide them. A stratum on which the metric collapses along itself is a single projector; a fold is silent only at first order and moves at second, and the bending of every geodesic is a quantum metric dipole. The construction extends to mixed states through the symmetric logarithmic derivative. Applied to public data from a superconducting heat engine and a Bose–Einstein condensate, a three-level standard for extracting angles shows that single eigenvectors trade identity where their gap is unresolved while the subspace keeps it. These data test the stability of the subspace, the reason for building the geometry on the projector, rather than the tensor itself. The Davis–Kahan bound, read as a rule for what can be looked at separately and what only as a whole, ties every result together.

1 Introduction and Foundational Underpinnings

The variation of eigenstates under deformations of a self-adjoint operator is a central theme in mathematical physics. The rigorous framework for tracking such variations was established by Tosio Kato through his development of analytic perturbation theory for linear operators, building on the functional calculus and resolvent methods of Frigyes Riesz [Kato 1995]. Kato showed that when a finite subset of the spectrum remains isolated from the rest by a contour in the complex plane, the corresponding spectral projector varies analytically with the operator. This projector-valued formulation provides a globally smooth description of spectral subspaces and naturally circumvents the technical difficulties associated with individual, possibly degenerate, eigenvectors.

In modern condensed matter and quantum information physics, the geometric consequences of this spectral sensitivity are captured by the Quantum Geometric Tensor [Provost–Vallee 1980; Berry 1984]. Conventionally, the tensor is introduced parametrically on a manifold of external parameters, such as crystal momentum in the Brillouin zone. Its imaginary part yields the Berry curvature, whose integral over closed manifolds produces topological invariants, while its real part defines a Riemannian quantum metric that governs fidelity susceptibility, orbital magnetism and Wannier localisation.

Despite its success, the parametric formulation inherently mixes two distinct geometric structures: the intrinsic geometry of the state manifold and the arbitrary choice of coordinates on the parameter space. To disentangle them, we develop a coordinate-free formulation in which the full tensor is defined intrinsically on the tangent bundle of the Grassmannian manifold of rank- orthogonal projectors. Using the Riesz–Kato resolvent identity, we show that both the quantum metric and the Berry curvature emerge directly from a single canonical Hermitian form on this manifold.

A central result of this approach is that every admissible tangent deformation of a spectral projector is generated exclusively by virtual transitions across the spectral gap. This structural constraint leads to exact spectral decompositions of both the metric and the curvature in terms of interband matrix elements weighted by inverse energy gaps. It also implies a sharp inequality relating the Berry curvature to the quantum metric, establishing that geometric phase effects are quantitatively bounded by the strength of cross-gap susceptibility.

Furthermore, we show that the intrinsic quantum metric controls the cost of non-adiabatic driving. The metric is the quantum Fisher information of the moving subspace; a bath converts that speed into dissipation, and the friction carried by the pairs that rotate the projector is the intrinsic metric reweighted pair by pair by the spectrum and the bath. The excess work generated by finite-rate driving is then bounded from below by the thermodynamic length measured with this metric, with an explicit spectral prefactor. This provides a direct geometric origin for dissipative costs in driven quantum systems.

By anchoring the construction in operator theory rather than band parameters, the framework reveals that physical parameter spaces do not generate quantum geometry; they select finite-dimensional trajectories through a pre-existing Grassmannian geometry. Two consequences follow that are invisible in coordinates. Transport tensors of every order are pullbacks of one cross-gap structure, so that the quantum metric dipole, the nonlinear Hall response and the orbital moment are the same pair sum weighted differently. And where the pullback degenerates, the intrinsic geometry decides what happens: geodesics of the pullback metric refract with an index equal to the rate at which the subspace rotates, is reflected where that rotation stops, and is guided where the gap narrows instead. The kinds of stratum are told apart by order: where the metric has a kernel, the second derivative of the projector is itself a tangent vector, and it decides whether the kernel ever opens.

Every inequality in the paper is sharp, and we determine when each is met. Equality is rigid in every case: it is reached only by couplings of one strength across one gap, by a rigid rotation at fixed gap, by motion at constant intrinsic speed, on a complex line of the Grassmannian, or, for permutations, by involutions. The equality cases are proved alongside their inequalities, and their algebraic cores are checked in Lean.

Several statements here are coordinate-free recastings of established results, and we say so where they appear: the metric–curvature inequality is the determinant inequality of band geometry and its saturation the Kähler or ideal-band condition; the pullback description of the band metric and curvature is standard; the stability of subspaces against perturbation is the Davis–Kahan theorem; the redistribution flow is Brockett's double-bracket flow. Each is included because the projector formulation makes its proof, or its scope, transparent, and because later sections rest on it.

The paper is organised as follows. Section 2 introduces the intrinsic quantum geometric tensor on the Grassmannian. Section 3 derives its explicit spectral realisation. Section 4 shows how conventional parametric expressions arise as pullbacks and where the pullback degenerates. Section 5 establishes the spectral lower bound on dissipation. Section 6 derives the metric–curvature inequality and its geometric consequences, and determines when every bound in the paper is met. Section 7 builds the transport tensors, Section 8 treats geodesic refraction across degenerate strata, and Section 9 extends the construction to mixed states. Section 10 sets out a standard for extracting angles from raw data and applies it to two experiments. Section 11 discusses the results, Section 12 draws them together as one law read at two grains, separately and as a whole, and Section 13 concludes. Technical details and explicit examples are collected in the appendices.

3 Spectral Realization of Tangent Deformations

For clarity, we first derive the explicit spectral formulas in the case of an isolated discrete spectrum; the operator statements extend to the general setting without change (Remark 3.8). To evaluate the intrinsic geometric tensor and its components, the abstract tangent vectors must be resolved into explicit, computable spectral identities. This section evaluates the contour integrals that define the first-order response of a spectral projector under an arbitrary operator perturbation.

4 Parametric Realization (Pullback Structure)

The intrinsic quantum geometric tensor constructed on the Grassmannian is independent of any auxiliary parameter space. In physical applications, however, one is typically given a smooth family of Hamiltonians parameterized by points of a manifold . This section shows how the familiar coordinate expressions for the quantum metric and Berry curvature arise as the pullback of the intrinsic tensor under the map induced by the family.

5 Spectral Lower Bounds on Dissipation

One of the most direct physical applications of the intrinsic quantum metric is a lower bound on the cost of non-adiabatic driving. The metric measures how fast a spectral subspace is being moved; a bath charges for that motion. This section makes both halves precise. The first half is kinematic and needs nothing beyond Sections 2–4: the metric is the quantum Fisher information of the moving subspace, and the gap limits how quickly the subspace can be moved. The second half needs a declared bath, and there the metric reappears, reweighted pair by pair by the spectrum, as a lower bound on the excess work.

Let be a family of self-adjoint operators driven along a smooth path over the time interval , with the gap open throughout, and write , so that .

5.1 The quantum Fisher information of a moving subspace

Lemma 5.1 (Fisher information of the subspace). Let be the normalised state supported on the moving subspace. Its symmetric logarithmic derivative is , and its quantum Fisher information is

In particular, for , .

Proof. The symmetric logarithmic derivative is defined by . Differentiating the projector identity with respect to time gives the linearised relation , which is satisfied identically by the choice . Substituting into the Fisher information gives . Because is a tangent vector, it is strictly off-diagonal, ; squaring isolates the two diagonal blocks, which contribute equally to the trace, so . ∎

The intrinsic metric is therefore the information-geometric speed of the subspace: it measures how distinguishable the state becomes per unit time, and so how much the driving must change. It does not by itself measure dissipation. Moving unitarily leaves the spectrum of fixed, so its von Neumann entropy is constant and no entropy is produced; the Fisher metric here is the symmetric-logarithmic-derivative metric, while near-equilibrium thermodynamic length uses the Kubo–Mori metric and a relaxation time that no purely geometric quantity supplies. Turning speed into cost requires a bath (Section 5.3).

6 Metric–Curvature Inequalities, Equality and Rigidity

The preceding sections established that the intrinsic Quantum Geometric Tensor admits a canonical decomposition into its symmetric metric component and antisymmetric curvature component, . While these objects are traditionally presented as independent geometric quantities in parametric band theory, the coordinate-free projector formulation reveals a structural constraint: the generation of a geometric phase is quantitatively bounded by the intrinsic metric of the Grassmannian tangent bundle. In coordinates the bound below is the determinant inequality , standard in the band-geometry literature [Roy 2014; Mera–Ozawa 2021]; the projector formulation makes both its proof and its saturation transparent, and no priority is claimed for it.

6.1 The geometric angle safeguard

Expressing the metric inner product as , where is the geometric angle between the two tangent deformations, turns (6.1) into

This dependence is a directional safeguard: the curvature a pair of deformations can generate is limited by how far apart they point in the intrinsic metric. The control it gives is relative, not absolute. Near a degeneracy both sides of (6.2) diverge at the same rate — a two-level system saturates the bound at every gap, so the ratio stays one as the gap closes — and the inequality is not a regularisation. The suppression at is a property of antisymmetry, since any 2-form vanishes on proportional arguments.

6.2 Control hierarchy

Both geometric quantities are driven by the same interband transition amplitudes across the spectral cut (Theorem 3.6). The quantum metric quantifies the total capacity of the transport channels; the Berry curvature tracks the phase interference among them; and the metric is the quantitative envelope for every admissible curvature. Metric rigidity therefore enforces curvature rigidity: if then and , and if a perturbation has no cross-gap coupling, for every , then it moves nothing and carries no curvature. The ordering is one of control, not of generation: cross-gap transitions generate both and , and bounds .

With Euclidean on a Brillouin zone, (6.4) is the trace condition of ideal bands [Roy 2014]. With the round metric of the parameter sphere, both bands of Appendices B and C meet it with equality at every point: the two-level band has and , the lowest spin-1 band and (both to ). Breaking the spin-1 symmetry with lifts it strictly above, by 0.04 to 0.46 over the sample. The same equality holds for the lowest band in every spin , which is the lowest Landau level on a sphere (Appendix C). Equality in both steps means the map is conformal and its image is a complex line at every point, which is what a holomorphic band is.

Example 6.5 (A loop that comes back still remembers). Carry the lower two-level band once around the circle of polar angle . The projector returns exactly to where it started (to ), so no measurement of the final subspace can tell that the loop happened. The state vector does not return: it comes back multiplied by the Berry phase (enclosed solid angle) , computed from overlaps around the loop as . The phase is the curvature of this section integrated over the cap, . The subspace is back where it began; the history of the path is kept only in the phase, and only the curvature can write it there.

7 Geometric Transport Tensors as Pullbacks

Quantities such as the quantum metric dipole, the nonlinear Hall conductivity and the orbital magnetisation are usually computed in a band basis on a chosen parameter space. In the present framework each of them is read off the same cross-gap data that define : the pairs with , weighted by powers of their gaps, together — at second order — with the rotation of the eigenvectors inside each sector. This section makes that statement exact for each tensor.

7.1 The quantum metric dipole

The quantum metric dipole measures the variation of the quantum metric across the parameter manifold, . Differentiating the pullback gives (4.5),

and differentiating the constraint gives the second-order response equation . With the exact second variation (4.6), (7.1) is the complete dipole. To resolve it in the eigenbasis, write in the instantaneous eigenbasis and . Holding the eigenvectors fixed and differentiating only the operator and the gaps gives the two-index form

with by Hellmann–Feynman. The eigenvectors also turn: contains, besides , the rotation terms

and for a spectrum that is nondegenerate within each sector the dipole is exactly

The rotation sum runs over every level , including those in the same sector as or : these are the three-state terms, and they live in exactly the off-diagonal block that survives the trace in (7.1). On forty random families (7.3) reproduces the contour value of (7.1) to , while the two-index form (7.2) alone can be off by more than a factor of a hundred where its terms cancel. The dipole is therefore controlled by the cross-gap channels, the gap variations and the rotation of the eigenvectors within each sector — the last being the second-order content that Proposition 4.3 isolates.

7.2 One pair sum, many weights

Take a nondegenerate ground state , gaps , and for each excited level the pair metric and pair curvature

so that and by Theorem 3.6. The responses of transport theory are the same pair sums with different weights in the gap:

QuantityPair sumWeightChecked against
quantum metricTheorem 3.6

The metric family and the curvature family each run through the powers of the gap. The nonlinear Hall input sits one power below the metric, the static response one power above, and the orbital moment one power above the curvature. Which power a measurement selects tells which part of the cross-gap geometry it reads, and fixes how it behaves at a closing gap (Section 7.5). With , the static response function, the friction of Section 5 is read directly from it: for pure relaxation and with precession (to on 200 random systems) — the familiar statement that a friction coefficient is a response function evaluated at the bath's rate, written in the spectral weights of this paper.

7.3 Nonlinear Hall conductivity

The second-order current generated in the absence of a magnetic field has an intrinsic, scattering-time-independent part fixed by quantum geometry. Its input is not the quantum metric itself but the Berry connection polarizability, the band-normalised metric

which for an isolated band is the pair sum with weight of the table above. The intrinsic conductivity is built from its dipoles [Gao–Yang–Niu 2014; Kaplan–Holder–Yan 2024]:

In the language of this paper, (7.4) is the dipole of a pullback: the same cross-gap pairs as , weighted one power of the gap lower, differentiated along the Brillouin zone. The second-order machinery of Section 7.1 — the exact second variation and the rotation terms — is what its spectral evaluation requires; a form that differentiates only the operator and the gaps misses the same three-state terms as (7.2).

7.4 Orbital magnetisation

The orbital moment of a Bloch state is the curvature-family pair sum weighted by one power of the gap, (table above), so orbital magnetism belongs to the antisymmetric half of the cross-gap geometry. A nonlinear orbital response is the field derivative of that kernel; its full second-order expression, which needs the second-order machinery of Section 7.1 applied to the curvature family, is not derived here.

7.5 Singular nodes and regularisation

When the gap closes the denominators diverge, each tensor at the rate set by its weight. Following each quantity toward the charge-neutral point with everything else fixed (Figure 9), the metric and the curvature diverge as , the dipole one power faster as , the zero-temperature rotation friction as , and the finite-temperature friction not at all, since the population difference closes with the gap. The measured slopes are .

A finite quasiparticle lifetime enters through a complex regularisation , , in the interband denominators,

which replaces the poles by Lorentzian profiles. is not self-adjoint — carries where carries — so it is not a tangent vector, and the metric, Gram positivity and real angles of Sections 2–6 do not apply to it. What the prescription defines is a retarded response, and the modulus-squared weight that follows from it is the correct regularised weight for response calculations. The regularised pair sum stays below even at a closed gap and returns the metric as on an open one. Applied to the two-index form (7.2), the regularisation gives

whose gap-derivative term is the derivative of the regularised weight , exactly as the term in (7.2) is the derivative of . It vanishes with the gap, and the singularity becomes a peak at of height times ; the rotation terms of (7.3) are regularised the same way. Lifetimes near nodes proper require a non-Hermitian or Lindblad formulation, which is a different theory.

8 Geodesic Refraction Across Degenerate Strata

The metric–curvature inequality governs the magnitude of geometric phase effects but does not prescribe how geometric transport continues across loci where the effective rank of the pulled-back tensor changes. By Proposition 4.1 the pullback metric may degenerate on codimension-one strata of without the spectral gap closing. The established band-geometry literature assumes this does not happen — the map into the Grassmannian is taken to be an immersion, so that throughout. This section asks what governs the geodesics of the pullback metric when that assumption fails. Geodesics are the object studied throughout: they are the paths a transport calculation would follow, not a measurement of transport.

8.1 The refraction law

Suppose admits a Killing field tangent to a family of hypersurfaces, the interfaces; let be the coordinate along the Killing direction and transverse to it, so that . Let be the angle, measured in , between a trajectory and the interface normal.

Proposition 8.1 (Variational refraction). Along any geodesic of ,

Proof. The Lagrangian is independent of , so is conserved. For a unit-speed geodesic the along-interface component of the velocity is , whence . Squaring gives the second form. ∎

Across two sides of an interface, (8.1) is the sine-squared refraction law , with rigidity . It is Clairaut's relation, and therefore Snell's law with refractive index . Three consequences fix the reading. The sine-squared form is the square of ordinary Snell, not an independent law. There is no separate index to introduce: Fermat's principle with as the metric yields (8.1) directly. And the quantity playing the role of the index is , the metric component along the interface — not the smallest eigenvalue of , and not its reciprocal. Near a degenerate stratum the collapsing direction is the along-interface direction, so and coincide there; a rule written with is correct in the regime where it is usually applied and fails away from it (Figure 11).

8.2 The index is a subspace rotation rate

Proposition 8.2. For subspaces with principal angles , . Since , to leading order for a single principal angle, and the refractive index is the rate at which the occupied subspace rotates as one moves along the interface.

Refraction in this setting is therefore not an optical analogy imported from outside. The trajectory bends because the subspace rotates at different rates on the two sides of the stratum, and appears because the Hilbert–Schmidt metric on is itself a sum of squared sines of principal angles.

8.3 Total internal reflection

Proposition 8.3 (Total internal reflection at a degenerate stratum). Let be the conserved quantity of (8.1). Since , a geodesic can only visit points where . A trajectory with cannot reach a stratum on which : it turns at the locus , where and the velocity is tangent to the interface. Only trajectories with , already exactly normal, reach the stratum.

The degenerate stratum is repulsive: generic transport does not approach it, and is turned away before reaching it. This is the directional protection of the geometry, correctly stated; the mechanism is the caustic of a metric whose along-interface component vanishes, the same as total internal reflection in optics.

8.4 A solvable test

Take the two-band operator with , , so that the spectral gap equals 2 everywhere: any degeneration of the pulled-back metric is failure of immersion, not a closing gap. The metric computed from by central differences is to , and equals the principal angle between and , computed from eigenvector overlaps with no trace identity, to (Proposition 8.2). The full geodesic system, integrated from at with no conservation law imposed, crosses the branch switch of at ; along it drifts by , while drifts by and by . A geodesic launched inward from at has and a predicted turning point ; the integrated trajectory turns at with — grazing incidence, not normal. Over incidences from to every trajectory turns before the stratum; the exactly normal one passes through it.

Remark 8.4 (What bends a geodesic is a metric dipole). The geodesic equation is driven by the Christoffel symbols, and those of the first kind are half-sums of derivatives of the metric: is the quantum metric dipole of Section 7.1. In the coordinates of Proposition 8.1 the only transverse force is , and in the test above, computed from the projector by finite differences, it agrees with the dipole to . The bending of this section and the dipole responses of Section 7 are therefore the same derivative of the same metric, read once as a force on a path and once as a transport coefficient.

8.5 Two kinds of degenerate stratum

Let be a connected interface on which is degenerate, with along and across it. Which direction collapses decides everything that follows.

Lemma 8.5 (A stratum on which nothing moves). On , if and only if , if and only if is constant along : the whole interface maps to one point of .

Proof. vanishes only when . A curve with zero derivative on a connected interval is constant. The converse is immediate. ∎

So a degenerate stratum is one of two kinds. It is polar if the kernel of is tangent to it: then, by Lemma 8.5, is constant along it, and the refraction law with its total internal reflection applies. The stratum of Section 8.4 is polar: the whole line is one projector. It is a fold if the kernel points across it while keeps moving along it, as on the Bloch sphere with , where on while . The two are the null-hypersurface and caustic cases of the singularity theory of maps.

The first-order metric cannot tell the two apart beyond the direction of its kernel. The next order can.

Proposition 8.6 (The first order at which a silent direction moves). Let be a silent direction at a point, , and let be the first order with . Then is block off-diagonal, so it is itself a tangent vector, and along the line through the point in direction

where is the chordal distance of Proposition 8.2. If is even, and agree to order : two sheets of the family meet, and the direction is a fold. If is odd, they separate at order : the family passes through, and the reparametrisation removes the silence.

In the fold above, at , exactly, the diagonal blocks of vanish to , and the ratio of to the leading term of (8.3) is , , at ; along the polar stratum the projector drifts by over the whole line (Figure 12). Remark 8.7 (What a fold needs). The Christoffel symbols (8.2) are contracted with , and both kinds of stratum make them diverge: at the polar stratum of Section 8.4, ; at the fold above, where , . At a polar stratum this is harmless, because the conserved quantity of (8.1) keeps every trajectory with away from it. At a fold nothing does: the Clairaut constant contains only, does not vanish there, trajectories reach the fold at every incidence, and the geodesics of alone are not determined across it. The geodesic problem must be supplemented by a choice of direction in the kernel, which the degenerate metric does not supply. The same structure is basic in Carrollian geometry, where a degenerate metric describes a null hypersurface only together with a vector field in its kernel [Ciambelli–Jai-akson 2025]. Only the polar case is governed by Proposition 8.3.

Example 8.8 (Three bodies seen through their distances). Place three equal masses in the plane at , and form the Jacobi vectors , and the vector . The projector forgets the overall size and the planar rotation, which is the phase of , and keeps exactly the shape of the triangle: is the shape sphere of the three-body problem [Montgomery 2015]. Its Bloch vector has third component proportional to the signed area, so the collinear triangles form the great circle .

Now record the shape only through the normalised squared distances . They are linear in , and , so they see and and not the sign of : a triangle and its mirror image, , have the same distances (difference exactly 0). The metric that the distances pull back to the sphere is degenerate exactly on the collinear circle, where the ratio of its singular values is 0 (it is 0.24 at latitude 0.4). Its kernel points straight across the circle (latitude component ), while keeps moving along it (). To an observer who sees only distances, the collinear triangles are a fold: the two mirror sheets of the sphere meet there, and the direction that observer cannot see is the orientation of the triangle. The three-body motion itself runs on the nondegenerate round metric of the shape sphere, inherited from the mass metric, and that metric supplies exactly the structure the fold lacks (Figure 13).

8.6 When the gap narrows instead

The refraction law asks only for the pullback metric, so it applies unchanged when the index varies because the gap varies rather than because the image of the family folds. What changes is the direction of the effect. By Lemma 3.1 a fixed coupling divided by a smaller gap moves the projector faster, so where the gap narrows rises and the index rises with it. Trajectories then bend toward the normal, cross the narrow-gap line, and are turned back only where the index has fallen to their conserved level on either side: the narrow-gap line guides them as a graded-index fibre guides light.

In the family , the gap is narrowest on and the occupied projector never stops rotating: . A geodesic launched from at conserves to (the candidate drifts by ), crosses , and turns at , where the conserved level predicts (Figure 14). Total internal reflection is therefore a property of strata on which the subspace stops rotating, not of places where the gap closes.

10 From Raw Data to Intrinsic Angles

The framework makes three structural predictions that can be checked on measured data. Tangent deformations are strictly off-diagonal with respect to the instantaneous spectral decomposition. The spectral subspace keeps its identity while individual eigenvectors inside it are free to scramble. Transport angles are constrained by the metric–curvature inequality. Each of these is a statement about the projector, not about a basis. Data, however, arrive in a basis: the instrument's own. This section sets out how to get from one to the other, then applies it to two independent public datasets.

10.1 A standard for extracting angles

Laboratories process their data before publishing it. Readout axes are rotated and rescaled, correction matrices are applied, populations are fitted. Every such step changes raw angles while leaving the physics unchanged. An angle read directly off processed data therefore mixes two things: the system's geometry and the instrument's point of view. To separate them, every extracted angle is assigned one of three levels.

  1. Level 0, raw angle . The angle as the instrument's frame sees it, computed from the measured object with no model imposed.
  2. Level 1, geometric angle . What remains once the point of view is removed: the angle inside the intrinsic metric of the Grassmannian,
  3. Level 2, physical interpretation. A physical meaning is assigned only after has been obtained unambiguously.

The test that separates the first two levels is a change of frame. Under a unitary change of basis , , the geometric angle (10.1) does not move: every quantity in it is a trace. A raw angle between two readout vectors moves as soon as the readout axes are rescaled; rescaling one axis by a factor of two shifts a raw angle of by . Only what survives every change of view is a property of the system.

To make extractions comparable across datasets and across competing frameworks, every reported transport tensor should carry at least the four quantities of Table 10.1.

Table 10.1. Standard reporting for geometric transport extractions.
QuantitySymbolMeaning
Transport capacityTotal available geometric transport strength
Transport alignmentMutual orientation of two transport channels
Transport chiralityFraction of capacity convertible to curvature
Resulting curvatureMeasured or derived Berry or Uhlmann curvature

With these four numbers in hand, Theorem 6.1 becomes directly testable on data. Since , inequality (6.1) reads

This is (6.1) exactly, not a weaker form, and it is sharp on the same extremal partner. It says that curvature can only be produced from the part of the capacity that is perpendicular in the intrinsic metric. Any proposed alternative transport metric can then be compared with the intrinsic one on the same footing.

One further condition decides whether a Level 1 angle exists at all. A direction extracted as the leading eigenvector of an estimated operator is defined only as sharply as its eigenvalue is separated from the next. For a two-dimensional covariance with eigenvalues estimated from samples, the leading direction scatters by

radians. At this predicts , and for eigenvalue ratios 4, 1.2 and 1.02; direct simulation gives , and . As the ratio approaches one the direction becomes uniformly random and carries no information (Figure 15, left). A direction is reported only where its gap is resolved.

10.2 The tip and the tail: why the subspace is the observable

Formula (10.3) is one instance of a general law, and Section 3 already contains its infinitesimal form: by Proposition 3.5 the projector moves by at most , where is the gap that separates the whole subspace from the rest. The finite form follows from one identity.

Proposition 10.1 (Gap identity). Let and be self-adjoint, let be a spectral projector of and a spectral projector of , with and . Then

Proof. Using and , . Using and , . Subtract. ∎

The block measures how far the subspace has moved: its operator norm is the sine of the largest principal angle between and , where . Equation (10.4) is a Sylvester equation for that block. If the spectrum of on and the spectrum of on are separated by , it gives

the theorem of Davis and Kahan [Davis–Kahan 1970; Bhatia 1997]. It is a known result and is stated here because the rest of the section rests on it. On 2,000 random instances of sizes 3 to 8, (10.5) held every time, with the largest ratio of left to right side 0.998.

What (10.5) makes visible is that two different gaps govern two different objects.

  • The tip. A single eigenvector is a rank-one projector. Its is the distance to its nearest neighbour, which inside a cluster of close eigenvalues can be arbitrarily small.
  • The tail. The projector onto the whole cluster has its set by the distance from the cluster to the rest of the spectrum, which can be large while the internal splittings vanish.

Remark 10.2 (The tip is free at a tie). If and , then for all scalars .

This is linearity, and it is all the remark needs.

At an exact tie no single vector is selected; any perturbation, however small, picks one. In a six-level test with a doubly degenerate ground level, a perturbation of size turns the selected vector by a median of , while the projector onto the pair stays within its bound (10.5), never exceeding it. This is the mechanism behind the framework's central choice: the eigenvectors vote, and they can trade identity; the subspace keeps it. Geometry built on the projector inherits the stability of the tail. Geometry built on eigenvectors inherits the freedom of the tip.

Near a tie the freedom has a definite shape. For two levels with splitting and coupling , the upper eigenvector sits at mixing angle with

An eigenvector angle is a coupling-to-gap ratio. As is swept through zero, the two eigenvectors do not pass through each other: they trade places, and the upper one turns through a full inside a window of width about . Sampled at 29 points, as the heat-engine drive amplitudes are, a wide crossing never turns by more than in one step, while a crossing narrower than the sampling step shows up as a single jump of . A large single-step jump of a leading eigenvector is therefore the signature of a crossing or of a near-tie decided by noise. An independent split of the data separates the two: a real crossing jumps in both halves, while a noise-decided tie jumps at random.

10.3 Superconducting quantum heat engine readout

The first dataset is the public single-shot readout of a transmon quantum Otto engine [Uusnakki et al. 2025]. In the calibration set, 19,899 shots were recorded for each prepared state , , , each shot a point in the in-phase/quadrature (I–Q) readout plane. These are Level 0 objects: the plane is the instrument's.

Number of populations. A Gaussian mixture fitted to the pooled calibration shots is scored by the Bayesian information criterion. The score is lowest at four components (), against at three and at five. Three states were prepared and four populations are resolved. The fourth is a small component (weight ) with the most elongated covariance of the four, eigenvalue ratio 2.49. What it is physically is not tested here.

The core and the tail of one cloud. Within the ground-state cloud alone, split by distance from its mean:

  • The inner half (9,950 shots) is almost round, with eigenvalue ratio 1.076. By (10.3) its long axis is defined only to about , and because of the radial cut the realised scatter is larger still.
  • The outer tenth (1,990 shots) is clearly elongated, with ratio 2.216.

A noise model with the core's covariance shows which of these is real. Three hundred synthetic clouds were cut exactly as the data were.

  • Angle between the two axes. In the data it is . In the synthetic clouds it ranges from to (median , 99.9th percentile ). The angle is therefore not a Level 1 quantity: the core has no direction to compare against.
  • Elongation of the tail. In the synthetic clouds it never exceeds 1.27. The measured 2.22 lies far outside that band.

The tail has a shape that the noise does not have (Figure 16). That shape is a property of the data. Its direction is still read in the readout frame, so it remains Level 0 until a frame-free version is built.

What the tail is made of, and how it moves with the cycle. The same core/tail split applied to the engine shots, about the centre of all shots at one drive setting, separates the populations sharply. Early in the first stroke, while is high, the inner 90% of shots read as 0.722, 0.218, 0.059; the outer 10% read almost entirely as 0.623 and 0.369, with only 0.006. Late in the same stroke, as drains, the core moves to 0.569, 0.251, 0.173, and the tail's balance reverses to 0.387, 0.602. With about a thousand tail shots at each point, the shift of the share is close to eleven standard errors. The tail therefore tracks the engine: it is where the and populations live, and its make-up changes as the stroke proceeds. Reading these shots as ones caught mid-transition is a Level 2 interpretation and is not tested here.

The leading eigenvector along the cycle. Counting every shot of the three-cycle run into the four populations, and correcting the counts with the authors' own overlap-correction matrix, gives a clean 128-point trajectory through the engine strokes. In the first stroke it shows draining from 0.620 to 0.487 while rises from 0.111 to 0.182. The leading eigenvector of the population covariance over a sliding five-point window turns by per step on average on the corrected trajectory. On the uncorrected counts it averages , with isolated single-step jumps of and . By (10.6), single jumps near are what a crossing between samples produces, but they are also what a near-tie decided by shot noise produces.

Crossing or tie: the split-half test. The two readings make opposite predictions. A crossing is in the system, so if every setting's shots are divided into two independent halves, each half must jump at the same step. A tie decided by noise jumps at random places. Each half was given its own 128-point trajectory, both with and without the correction matrix, and the halves were formed twice: odd against even shots, and after shuffling the shot order. Before the run the test was checked on synthetic shots of the same layout: planted structure repeated in both halves, and pure shot noise did not. The kill condition, written in advance, was that fewer than half of one half's jumps (steps over ) recur in the other within one step, or that the number of recurrences does not exceed the 99th percentile of the count obtained by sliding one half along the other.

  • The full-data trajectories reproduce the notebook: a mean step of corrected and uncorrected, with the same largest jumps.
  • Odd/even, corrected: 20 and 14 jumps, 6 recurring, against 5.4 expected by chance (99th percentile 10). Uncorrected: 19 and 17, 5 recurring, against 6.7 (10.8).
  • Shuffled split, corrected: 23 and 12, 3 recurring, against 6.3 (12). Uncorrected: 21 and 17, 8 recurring, against 8.2 (12).
  • The step sizes of the two halves are uncorrelated: , , , .

The big jumps do not repeat beyond chance in any of the four comparisons. They are ties decided by shot noise, not crossings in the engine. That is itself the law of Section 10.2: a five-point window of populations has no resolved gap between its top two directions, so the leading eigenvector is the free tip, and noise casts its vote.

10.4 Dark solitons in a Bose–Einstein condensate

The second dataset is a different experiment entirely: the NIST dark-soliton image set [Fritsch et al. 2022]. It contains 16,478 absorption images of Rb condensates (11,913 from July and 4,565 from August), binned to 5,412 pixels and normalised by atom number. The images are split into two halves, either odd against even or at random, and the covariance of each half is diagonalised independently. The prediction for how far each rank- projector should move between halves is the first-order formula of Lemma 3.1 applied to the covariance difference :

Before use, this predictor was calibrated on synthetic data and returned a ratio of 1.00.

Results.

  • Agreement. The median ratio of measured to predicted motion is 1.00 for the odd/even split, and 1.08 and 0.99 for two random splits. A pure-noise control gives projectors that disagree by at rank 3.
  • Vector against subspace, rank 3, odd/even split. The third eigen-image turns by between halves. The rank-3 subspace that contains it moves by .
  • The gap law. The 36 rank cuts (12 ranks, 3 splits) were ordered by relative gap .
    • At every cut with relative gap at least 0.10, 18 of 18, the measured motion lies between 0.93 and 1.12 of the prediction.
    • Below 0.10 the ratio scatters from 0.10 to 7.82, because the halves' own noise reorders near-tied modes. At rank 10 the formula expects – and the measurement is –: modes 10 and 11 exchanged order.

Locked pairs. The spectrum carries near-degenerate pairs , and in every split. At the cut that closes each pair, the single vectors are loose while the subspace holds (Table 10.2; Figure 15, right).

Table 10.2. Angle between independent halves at the cut closing each pair (range over three splits).

The eigen-images make the pairs readable. Images 2–5, 7, 8 and 10–12 are stripe patterns across the long axis of the cloud, recording where the soliton sits. Each pair is two stripe patterns offset by a quarter period: a sine–cosine pair for one translation family, which is how principal components describe a feature that moves. Inside such a pair the two members are nearly tied, so the tip is free. The pair as a whole is separated from its neighbours, so the tail holds.

The months themselves differ. Between July and August the top eigen-image differs by , the eigenvalues differ by 9–60% at every rank, and first order holds at only 5 of 12 ranks. They are two different clouds, not two samples of one, and the analysis above is therefore made within the pooled set and its splits rather than across months.

Nothing in this subsection is new as a law: it is the gap law of Section 10.2, which is the Davis–Kahan theorem. What the data add is a measurement of it, in an experiment unrelated to the heat engine, with the vector and the subspace measured side by side on the same images: the vectors trade identity, the subspace keeps it.

10.5 What remains open

One test is specified but not yet run: a frame-free version of the readout-tail direction, obtained by rescaling the readout plane to equal noise in both quadratures before extracting the axis, so that a Level 1 angle can be stated. Its kill condition is written in advance.

11 Discussion and Outlook

The central achievement of this work is the construction of a fully coordinate-free quantum geometric tensor on the Grassmannian manifold of spectral projectors. Starting from the Riesz–Kato theory of isolated spectral subspaces, both the quantum metric and the Berry curvature emerge as natural components of a single intrinsic Hermitian form defined directly on the tangent bundle of . The formulation needs no local eigenvector gauge, no Berry connection and no coordinate chart on parameter space.

A key conceptual point is that the real and imaginary parts of the tensor are not independent objects. Both are generated by the same cross-gap virtual transitions between the spectral subspace of and its complement. The tangent-space constraint

makes this mechanism explicit and leads directly to the metric–curvature inequality of Section 6. That the metric bounds the curvature is not a coincidence of two quantities but a consequence of their common origin: they are the symmetric and antisymmetric parts of one object built from the same amplitudes. The inequality explains why Berry curvature and the topological phenomena built on it are suppressed when interband mixing is weak or the gap is large, and its control is relative: near a node both sides grow together, so it limits the curvature per unit of metric, not the curvature itself.

The framework also yields a lower bound on non-adiabatic dissipation, and the way it does so is part of the result. The intrinsic metric is the quantum Fisher information of the moving subspace, its information-geometric speed; on its own it measures how much the driving must change, not what that change costs. A bath turns speed into cost. For relaxation to the instantaneous Gibbs state, and equally for a detailed-balance bath, the friction carried by the pairs that move the projector is the intrinsic metric reweighted pair by pair by twice the population difference times the gap times a relaxation factor. At zero temperature this confines the cost to a band of the metric, and the excess work of a protocol is bounded below by the squared intrinsic length divided by the time allowed. The geometric response is thereby connected to thermodynamic irreversibility through an explicit, tested bath weight rather than an assumed proportionality.

From a broader perspective, the construction clarifies the geometric foundations of transport. Higher-order coefficients arise as coordinate-dependent pullbacks of structures intrinsic to the Grassmannian, not as primitive features of the parameter manifold. Section 7 makes this concrete: one sum over cross-gap pairs, read with different powers of the gap, gives the quantum metric, the Berry connection polarizability that drives the intrinsic nonlinear Hall effect, the static response, the rotation friction, the Berry curvature and the orbital-moment kernel. At first order every such quantity factors through the gap. At second order the factorisation acquires a remainder from the rotation of the eigenvectors inside each sector, which is what the exact dipole (7.3) contains, and a direction that does not move the subspace at all can still change how far the other directions move it.

The refraction results of Section 8 deserve a closing comment, since a Snell-type law arising in an operator-theoretic setting invites more interpretation than it can carry. The law is Clairaut's relation for geodesics of the pullback metric, and its content lies in the identification of the index: what refracts a geodesic is a change in the rate at which the occupied subspace rotates. The sine squared that appears is not an additional structure; it is inherited from the fact that the Hilbert–Schmidt distance between projectors is a sum of squared sines of principal angles. The sharpest statements are the two that fix the scope. Where the subspace stops rotating along an interface, the stratum is one projector, it is repulsive, and trajectories turn back by total internal reflection. Where instead the gap narrows while the subspace keeps rotating, the index rises, and trajectories cross and are guided. A fold, where the collapse is transverse and the projector keeps moving along the locus, is crossed freely, and there the degenerate metric does not by itself determine the connection along which transport is computed. The two kinds are separated by order (Proposition 8.6): a polar stratum is silent at every order, a fold only at the first. The bending itself is a metric dipole (Remark 8.4), so the refraction of Section 8 and the transport tensors of Section 7 are two readings of one derivative of the metric.

Each bound in the paper is also rigid, and the equality cases (Theorem 6.3) are as informative as the bounds. The gap bound is met only by couplings of one strength across one gap; the speed limit only by a rigid rotation at fixed gap; the dissipation floor only by motion at constant intrinsic speed, so that the cheapest protocol follows a geodesic at constant speed; the curvature bound only on a complex line, through the exact deficit identity (6.3); and the permutation sandwich only by involutions. In each case the configuration that meets the bound is reconstructed from the fact that it meets it. This is the pattern of rigidity theorems in geometric analysis. A recent manuscript on spacetime Penrose inequalities, posted as an unrefereed preprint, follows the same pattern at much greater depth: equality there forces Schwarzschild data, and in the anti-de Sitter case a nonnegative second-order deficit has a finite-dimensional kernel that is resolved at fourth order [OpenAI 2026a]. The parallel here is one of structure only, and nothing in this paper depends on that manuscript. Here the second-order deficit (6.3) is exact and its kernel is the complex line, so no higher order is needed for the curvature bound; the step to higher order appears instead at the silent directions of a degenerate stratum (Proposition 8.6), where the kernel of the metric is resolved at second order in the projector and fourth order in the squared distance.

The data of Section 10 close the loop with experiment. In two unrelated systems — the readout of a superconducting heat engine and absorption images of a Bose–Einstein condensate — single leading eigenvectors are free wherever their gap is not resolved: in the engine their large jumps do not repeat across independent halves of the data, and in the condensate a single eigen-image turns by tens of degrees between halves while the subspace containing it moves by what the gap formula predicts, within 0.93–1.12 of it at every resolved gap. That is the reason, measured rather than assumed, for building the geometry on the projector: the vectors trade identity, the subspace keeps it.

Several directions are left open. The non-abelian sector (Remark 4.2) requires lifting the construction from to the Stiefel bundle, where the traceless part of the curvature lives. Transport through a fold requires a choice of kernel vector field or Ehresmann connection before the geodesic problem can be posed; the three-body example of Section 8.5 shows one natural choice, the round metric of the shape sphere, but no general rule is given here. The refraction tests of Section 8 hold the gap open or let it narrow; whether the index law survives when the gap closes exactly, where the projector itself ceases to be defined, is not determined here. The mean Uhlmann curvature dipole of Section 9 is written as an operator identity but not evaluated spectrally, and the full nonlinear orbital magnetisation tensor is not derived. On the experimental side, a frame-free version of the readout-tail direction would turn the one remaining Level 0 observation of Section 10 into a Level 1 angle.

12 Separately and as a Whole

Every object in this paper is a subspace held in place by a gap. The quantum metric measures how fast that subspace moves; the curvature measures how it turns; the friction measures what its motion costs; the refractive index is the rate at which it rotates; the data of Section 10 measure whether it holds still between independent halves of an experiment. Read together, the sections say one thing at two grains, and this closing section draws it out.

12.1 One law at two grains

Section 10.2 stated the gap identity and its consequence, the theorem of Davis and Kahan. Read as a statement about what can be looked at, it says the following. Take a cluster of levels separated from the rest of the spectrum by an outer gap , and let the levels inside the cluster be separated from each other by inner gaps . Under a perturbation ,

The cluster as a whole is held by the outer gap; each member separately is held only by its nearest neighbour. When the members swing while the whole stays put. We call the single vector the tip and the cluster subspace the tail: tips swing, the tail holds, and the outer gap sets the width of the corridor the tail can move in.

Figure 17 (left) shows this on a seven-level operator with a three-level cluster, the outer gap fixed at 3 and a perturbation of norm . As the inner gap falls from 1 to 0.01, the median turn of one vector inside the cluster rises from to , following , while the cluster subspace stays at –, below its bound in every one of 900 trials. Levels that sit together fuse into one object; the gap decides where one object ends and the next begins.

The same law governs motion in time. Theorem 5.2 bounds the speed of a subspace by the drive divided by the gap, . Figure 17 (right) follows a driven three-level path: the metric speed stays under the ceiling everywhere, and the two approach where the gap is narrowest. A two-level off-diagonal drive reaches the ceiling exactly. Whether the question is how far a subspace can be pushed by a perturbation or how fast it can be driven, the answer is set by the gap that encloses it.

Remark 12.1 (Two rhythms that become one). The same threshold appears when two oscillators lock. In the Kuramoto model of two phase oscillators with natural frequencies differing by and coupling , the phase difference obeys , and the pair locks into one rhythm exactly when [Kuramoto 1984]; integrated directly, locks and does not. The two-level operator with detuning and coupling has mixing angle , which equals at the same threshold. Both are governed by the single ratio of coupling to splitting: below one the two members are separate, above it they act as one. This is a correspondence of one ratio, not a derivation of one model from the other.

Example 12.2 (Light going both ways round a ring). In a ring cavity, light at one longitudinal order runs both ways, and the forward and backward modes span one two-dimensional subspace: the pair is the tail, and a single mode inside it is a tip. The outer gap is the free spectral range to the next order. The inner gap is set by two things that compete. Rotation splits the two directions by the Sagnac frequency ; scattering couples them with strength . The pair's own levels are then , , and the modes inside it mix at the angle : standing waves when scattering wins, travelling waves when rotation wins, crossing exactly at . Both mirrors moving together only slides the standing-wave pattern, the tip running while the tail holds, as the condensate's stripes do in Section 12.3.

In a four-mode model of two orders (, ) under random perturbations of norm 0.002, the single lowest mode turns by when scattering dominates and by when rotation dominates, falling as (log-log slope ), while the pair turns by at every rotation rate, below its bound in all 720 draws (Figure 18). In an active ring laser the same competition is nonlinear: the phase difference between the two beams obeys Adler's equation , and the beams lock to one frequency when ; integrated directly, locks and does not. This is the lock-in of the ring-laser gyroscope [Aronowitz 1971], and it is Remark 12.1 again: below the threshold the two directions act as one, and only the pair can be read; above it the directions separate, and each tip is measurable. The example reproduces known optics in the language of this section; it adds no new result about ring lasers.

12.2 How each part reads under it

  • The tangent law (Section 2). A subspace can only move by mixing across its own boundary: is block off-diagonal. Motion inside the cluster does not move the tail at all.
  • The gap bound (Section 3). Proposition 3.5 is (12.1) at first order: the tail moves by at most .
  • Pullbacks and silent directions (Section 4). A direction that only reshuffles levels inside the cluster is silent: it leaves the tail unmoved at first order, though at second order it changes how far the other directions move it.
  • Dissipation (Section 5). The friction is a sum over pairs straddling the outer gap, each weighted by its own gap; the speed limit is the ceiling of Figure 17.
  • The curvature bound (Section 6). Curvature lives in the sine between two directions of the tail's motion; it cannot exceed what the metric allows.
  • Transport tensors (Section 7). One sum over the same cross-gap pairs, read with different powers of the gap.
  • Degenerate strata (Section 8). The refractive index is the rotation rate of the tail. Where the tail stops rotating, trajectories turn back; where the gap narrows and the tail turns faster, they are guided.
  • Mixed states (Section 9). The symmetric logarithmic derivative exists exactly when the variation has no block inside the kernel: the same boundary that decides what moves.

12.3 Looking separately, then as a whole

This gives a working rule for any data set, and it is the rule Section 10 followed. First look at each part separately: compute every eigenvector and every gap on independent halves of the data, and ask of each direction whether its own gap is resolved. Then look at the whole: cut the spectrum only where a gap is resolved, and treat everything above the cut as one subspace. A part is reported only where its own gap holds it; a whole is reported at every resolved gap. Nothing is lost by this. What cannot be named separately is still measured, as part of the whole that contains it.

The condensate data show the rule at every cut (Figure 19). On the odd/even split, the single eigen-image and the rank- subspace move together wherever the cut falls on a resolved gap. Inside each near-degenerate pair they part company:

  • at , the cut that closes the pair , the third eigen-image turns by and the subspace by ;
  • at it is against ;
  • at , against .

At the cut inside a pair () the subspace inherits the free vector and turns with it, to within a degree. Across all three splits, every cut with relative gap at least 0.10 lands within 0.93–1.12 of the gap prediction, 18 of 18; every cut that misses it sits at a near-tie, with relative gap below 0.10.

The pairs themselves say what "the whole" is. The relative gap inside the pair is 0.03; at its outer edge it is 0.30. Eigen-images 2 and 3 are two stripe patterns offset by a quarter period, the sine and cosine of one moving pattern, and the soliton position oscillates in hold time at 2.70 Hz. A combination is the stripe at phase of its swing. The two directions inside the pair are nearly tied, so each half of the data picks its own combination of them, and the tip is free; the plane the two images span is the motion itself, and it holds. Sharp gaps make sharp subspaces: ten eigen-images carry half of all the variation in 16,478 images, and the participation of the spectrum is 26.5 against 1,911 for noise of the same spread.

The same rule, applied where no gap is resolved, gives the other half of the answer. In the heat-engine populations a five-point window has no resolved gap between its top two directions, and the leading eigenvector's large jumps do not repeat across independent halves of the shots. There the honest report is that no single direction exists at that grain. That is a measurement too.

12.4 The same geometry in a deck of cards

The rule applies wherever a distance is read off subspaces, and one such place is the Hamming metric on permutations that underlies the soficity question [Chapman–Lubotzky 2025; Beasley 2026]. For a permutation matrix of degree , let be the orthogonal projector onto its graph, the column space of . Then

where are the principal angles between the two graphs and over the eigenphases of . The proof is two lines: has off-diagonal blocks and its adjoint, so ; and has singular values . The card count is therefore a chordal distance between two points of the Grassmannian.

The intrinsic metric adds the geodesic. Along the graph projector moves with constant speed in the metric of Section 2, so its intrinsic length from to is

the Grassmannian geodesic distance (agreement on 20 random permutations, with the speed constant along each path). The count reads ; the intrinsic length reads . They see the same angles weighted differently, and the difference is the arrangement the count forgets. On twenty points, five disjoint swaps and one 10-cycle both move ten points and both give ; the swaps place five angles at , the cycle spreads its angles from to in steps of , and the intrinsic lengths are and (Figure 20). Per point the two are tied together by [Beasley 2026], which held on 2,000 random pairs. So the geodesic separates arrangements, but it still vanishes with the defect, and like every native reading of the Hamming metric it obstructs nothing. A recently claimed obstruction to soficity is of a different kind: an unrefereed manuscript constructs a finitely presented torsion-free group whose group algebra over is not directly finite [OpenAI 2026b], and sofic groups always have directly finite group algebras [Elek–Szabó 2004], so that group would not be sofic. The obstruction there is algebraic, not a reading of a distance.

The tip and the tail are visible here too. The displacement Gram of an -cycle has eigenvalues , which coincide for and : a cyclic motion comes in sine–cosine pairs, exactly as the condensate's moving stripes do in Section 12.3. Five swaps give the eigenvalue 2 five times over (and 0 five times), a complete tie in which no single mode is selected; the cycle resolves its modes into pairs. Each pair is a tail held by its gap; the vectors inside it are tips.

12.5 What the paper adds to the law

The bound is classical. What this paper adds is the reading of it as the organising principle of quantum geometry, and its use as a measuring rule:

  • the gap identity (10.4) written as a measuring rule, with its tie case (Remark 10.2), both checked in Lean;
  • the observation that every intrinsic quantity of Sections 2–9 is a property of the tail, held by the outer gap, and so inherits its stability;
  • the three-level standard of Section 10.1, which asks of every reported angle whether a gap holds it;
  • two independent public data sets in which the vector and the subspace were measured side by side, showing the tips trade identity while the tail keeps it.

Looked at separately, the parts of a quantum system are only as definite as the gaps between them. Looked at as a whole, the subspace above a resolved gap is definite, stable and measurable, and every geometric quantity in this paper is a quantity of that whole.

13 Conclusion

We have constructed a fully coordinate-free formulation of the Quantum Geometric Tensor on the Grassmannian manifold of rank- spectral projectors associated with a gapped self-adjoint operator. By building directly on the Riesz–Kato spectral projection formalism, we have shown that the geometry of an isolated spectral subspace can be expressed entirely at the level of the orthogonal projector, without reference to local eigenvector bases, Berry connections, coordinate charts or parameter-space constructions.

The intrinsic tensor

provides a unified geometric object whose symmetric component is the Hilbert–Schmidt quantum metric and whose antisymmetric component is the Berry curvature 2-form. Both arise from the canonical Hermitian form on the Grassmannian tangent bundle. The fundamental tangent-space constraint makes explicit that all geometric response is generated exclusively by virtual cross-gap excitations between the occupied and complementary spectral subspaces.

The real and imaginary parts of the tensor are therefore intertwined rather than independent. The same cross-gap matrix elements that determine the quantum metric also control the Berry curvature, which yields the sharp metric–curvature inequality of Section 6. Under an explicit bath model the intrinsic metric, reweighted by the spectrum, governs the minimal dissipative cost of finite-time driving, and gives a lower bound on the excess work in terms of the intrinsic length of the path. Every one of these bounds is sharp, and each is met only by one rigid configuration: one gap and one coupling strength, a rigid rotation, constant intrinsic speed, a complex line.

When applied to physical systems, the framework shows that parameter spaces do not generate geometric properties; they select finite-dimensional trajectories through a pre-existing Grassmannian geometry by pullback. This is why geometric transport is robust under smooth deformations of the Hamiltonian as long as the spectral gap stays open, and why, where the pullback degenerates, what happens next depends on whether the subspace has stopped rotating or the gap has narrowed.

By anchoring the construction in the functional-analytic foundations of analytic perturbation theory, the framework remains consistent across bounded matrix models and unbounded differential operators. It unifies perturbation theory, topological invariants, quantum thermodynamic geometry and the extraction of geometric angles from raw data within a single coordinate-free operator architecture.

The hypothesis holds for a wide class of physically relevant perturbations, including vector potentials entering differential operators and many-body interaction terms; the standard instance is the Kato–Rellich theorem, by which the Coulomb potential is relatively bounded with respect to the Laplacian with relative bound zero [Kato 1995; Reed–Simon 1975].

This saturation is forced: with and a one-dimensional complement, the blocks and of (2.1) are complex numbers, , and the Gram determinant in the proof of Theorem 6.1 vanishes identically. Every two-band pair is an extremal partner in the sense of Corollary 6.2.

This extremal case has been realised on a device. Gianfrate et al. measured the polarisation pseudospin of an exciton-polariton microcavity over the whole plane and computed the Berry curvature and all three metric components from its two angles [Gianfrate et al. 2020; Bleu et al. 2017]. Their maps are a direct measurement of (B.1) and (B.3) on a two-band system. They cannot, however, test the strict inequality: any curvature and metric computed from a unit pseudospin through its two angles satisfy at every point, whatever the field (to on an arbitrary smooth field with no Hamiltonian behind it). A device test of the strict inequality needs a measured tensor on three or more levels, where generic bands fall inside the bound (Appendix C). Coupled spins measured through their Rabi response, as in the nitrogen-vacancy experiment [Yu et al. 2020], are a setting that can supply one.

Introducing the angle between the tangent variations, , exposes the directional safeguard. As the node is approached, the metric components grow as and the curvature grows at the same rate, so the curvature per unit of metric stays fixed by : control is relative, as in Section 6.1. For collinear variations () the curvature vanishes identically however close the node is.

In spherical coordinates on the Bloch sphere the components reduce to the monopole values

and the first Chern number of the lower band is (quadrature: ). The coordinate-free construction therefore recovers the conventional parametric geometry and its topological integer exactly.

C Three-Band Model: Flat-Band Projections and Particle–Hole Duality

Consider the spin-1 operator

with eigenvalues and a flat middle band . For the rank-one projector onto the lowest band and the rank-two projector onto the lowest two bands, explicit computation gives identical intrinsic metrics:

The coefficient holds on 100 random configurations to for both ranks.

This establishes an exact particle–hole duality on the Grassmannian, and its mechanism has two parts. The first holds for every projector: , because is the tangent vector of and the metric is quadratic (Section 2; on 100 random rank-two projectors of size six with no flat band, the two agree to ). Hence , the metric of the top band. The second part is a property of the spin-1 spectrum: , so the top and bottom bands carry the same geometry. Together they give (C.1). The second part is what the flat, symmetric middle band supplies: adding a term , which breaks the symmetry, separates the two metrics (their ratio ranges from to over 50 configurations), while continues to hold exactly.

The lowest spin-1 band also saturates Theorem 6.1, exactly as the two-band model does (to on 200 random pairs). Saturation is not a two-band accident, but it is not generic either: for a three-band family with random Hermitian , the lowest band falls strictly inside the bound, with as small as one five-hundredth of the bound (Figure 21). The reason is holomorphy. The lowest band of is a spin coherent state: with and , it is proportional to (to on 200 random directions), the Veronese embedding of the sphere into . A band that depends on one complex coordinate of the parameter sphere in this way pulls the Fubini–Study form back to a Kähler form, and Kähler bands meet the determinant inequality with equality [Mera–Ozawa 2021]. A generic three-band family has no such coordinate, and falls strictly inside.

The same holds for every spin. The lowest band of in the spin- representation is the spin- coherent state, proportional to , the degree- Veronese embedding [Perelomov 1986]. Against the round metric of the parameter sphere it has and , so it meets Theorem 6.1 and the trace condition (6.4) with equality at every point, and its Chern number is . For the computed metric is to , both equalities hold to , and the Chern number is to ; adding lifts the trace condition strictly for every , by 0.03 to 0.27. These bands are physical: the spin- representation is the one-particle lowest Landau level on a sphere carrying flux quanta [Haldane 1983], so the lowest Landau level is the extremal case of the curvature bound in every flux.
